stem: Which is the best description of osmosis?

options.content: The movement of sugar molecules from a concentrated solution to a dilute solution
options.rationale: In osmosis it is water, not sugar, that moves.

options.content: The movement of water from a concentrated solution to a dilute solution through a partially permeable membrane
options.rationale: The direction is the wrong way round.

options.content: The net movement of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
options.rationale: Water, partially permeable membrane, dilute to concentrated.

options.content: The movement of any particles against a concentration gradient using energy
options.rationale: That describes active transport.

explanation: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.

stem: A Visking tubing bag containing distilled water is attached to a narrow glass tube and placed in a beaker of concentrated sucrose solution. What happens to the level of liquid in the glass tube?

options.content: It falls, because water leaves the bag by osmosis.
options.rationale: Water moves from the distilled water in the bag into the more concentrated sucrose solution outside.

options.content: It rises, because water enters the bag by osmosis.
options.rationale: Water moves out of the bag, towards the more concentrated solution outside.

options.content: It rises, because sucrose enters the bag.
options.rationale: Sucrose molecules are too large to pass through the tubing.

options.content: It stays the same, because the tubing is not alive.
options.rationale: Osmosis happens through any partially permeable membrane, living or not.

explanation: The sucrose solution outside is more concentrated than the distilled water inside the bag, so water moves out of the bag by osmosis. The volume inside the bag falls, so the level in the glass tube falls. Sucrose cannot enter because its molecules are too large to pass through the tubing.

stem: A strip of potato is left in a concentrated salt solution for an hour. What happens to it?

options.content: It gains mass and becomes firmer.
options.rationale: That happens in a dilute solution or water.

options.content: It gains mass and becomes softer.
options.rationale: Gaining water makes plant tissue firmer, not softer.

options.content: Its mass stays the same.
options.rationale: Water moves out because the solution is more concentrated than the cell sap.

options.content: It loses mass and becomes softer.
options.rationale: Water leaves the cells by osmosis into the more concentrated solution.

explanation: The salt solution is more concentrated than the cell sap, so water leaves the potato cells by osmosis. The strip loses mass and becomes soft and bendy.

stem: True or false: plant cells placed in pure water swell up and burst.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. The strong cell wall resists the pressure, so the cell becomes firm but does not burst.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. The cell wall stops plant cells from bursting; animal cells, with no wall, can burst.

explanation: Water enters plant cells in pure water by osmosis and the cells swell, but the cellulose cell wall resists the pressure, so they become firm (turgid) instead of bursting.

stem: True or false: in osmosis, water moves from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.

answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: water moves towards the more concentrated solution.

explanation: In osmosis, water moves from a dilute solution (more water) to a concentrated solution (less water) through a partially permeable membrane.

stem: A cylinder of sweet potato had a mass of 3.50 g. After 45 minutes in distilled water its mass was 3.92 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
explanation: Change $= 3.92 - 3.50 = 0.42$ g. Percentage change $= \dfrac{0.42}{3.50} \times 100 = +12\%$. The cylinder gained water by osmosis.

stem: A potato cylinder had a mass of 2.80 g before it was placed in a 1.0 mol/dm³ sucrose solution and 2.38 g afterwards. Calculate the percentage change in mass. Show a loss as a negative value.
explanation: Change $= 2.38 - 2.80 = -0.42$ g. Percentage change $= \dfrac{-0.42}{2.80} \times 100 = -15\%$. Water left the cells because the sucrose solution was more concentrated than the cell sap.
hints: The cylinder lost mass, so the answer is negative.

stem: Match each term with its description.

right.content: A plant cell full of water, with its contents pressing hard on the cell wall
A plant cell that has lost water and is soft, but whose membrane still touches the wall
The cytoplasm and membrane pulling away from the cell wall after a lot of water loss
The pressure of the cell contents pushing outwards on the cell wall
An animal cell bursting after taking in too much water

explanation: Turgid cells are full of water; turgor pressure is the push of the contents on the wall; flaccid cells have lost water and are soft; plasmolysis is when the membrane and cytoplasm pull away from the wall. Bursting describes animal cells, which have no wall.
hints: Turgid means swollen and firm; flaccid means soft and limp.

stem: Which statement about water potential is correct?

options.content: A concentrated sucrose solution has a higher water potential than pure water.
options.rationale: Adding solute lowers water potential.

options.content: Pure water has the highest water potential, and dissolving solutes lowers it.
options.rationale: This is why water moves from dilute to concentrated solutions.

options.content: Water moves from a lower water potential to a higher water potential.
options.rationale: It moves from higher to lower water potential.

options.content: Water potential is a measure of the number of solute molecules that can cross a membrane.
options.rationale: Water potential is about water, not solute crossing.

explanation: Pure water has the highest water potential. Adding solutes lowers it, so a concentrated solution has a low water potential. Water moves by osmosis from higher to lower water potential.
hints: Does dissolving sugar in water raise or lower its water potential?

stem: Red blood cells are placed in distilled water. What happens to them?

options.content: They shrink, because water leaves them by osmosis into the distilled water.
options.rationale: Water moves into the cells, which are more concentrated than distilled water.

options.content: Nothing, because the cell membrane stops water entering.
options.rationale: The cell membrane is partially permeable and lets water through.

options.content: They swell and burst, because water enters by osmosis and they have no cell wall.
options.rationale: Nothing resists the swelling.

options.content: They swell and become firm, like plant cells.
options.rationale: Without a cell wall, animal cells cannot resist the pressure and burst.

explanation: The cytoplasm of red blood cells is more concentrated than distilled water, so water enters by osmosis. Animal cells have no cell wall, so they swell until they burst.
hints: What stops a plant cell from bursting, and do red blood cells have it?

stem: What stops a plant cell from bursting when it takes in a lot of water?

options.content: The strong cellulose cell wall
options.rationale: The wall resists the pressure of the swelling contents.

options.content: The partially permeable cell membrane
options.rationale: The membrane is thin and would stretch and break on its own.

options.content: The large permanent vacuole full of cell sap
options.rationale: The vacuole fills with water and swells; it is the wall that resists the pressure.

options.content: The nucleus
options.rationale: The nucleus controls the cell; it does not resist pressure.

explanation: The cellulose cell wall is strong and only slightly elastic. As water enters, the cell contents press against it, but the wall stops the cell from bursting.

stem: Name the type of membrane that allows water molecules to pass through but not sucrose molecules.

rejected.feedback: A fully permeable membrane would let sucrose through too.
An impermeable membrane would not let water through either.
Be precise: the membrane is partially permeable.

explanation: A partially permeable (semi-permeable) membrane lets small molecules such as water through but stops larger molecules such as sucrose. Cell membranes and Visking tubing are partially permeable.

stem: Complete the sentences about water uptake by a root hair cell.

payload.template: The soil water is more {{blank:a}} than the cell sap of the root hair cell. Water therefore moves into the cell by {{blank:b}}, through the partially permeable cell {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Soil water is usually more dilute than cell sap, so water moves into root hair cells by osmosis through the partially permeable cell membrane. (The cell wall is fully permeable.)
hints: Which is more concentrated: the soil water or the cell sap?

stem:
Tendai placed discs of carrot in salt solutions of different concentrations for one hour and calculated the mean percentage change in mass.

| Salt concentration / mol per dm³ | 0.00 | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.40 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mean change in mass / % | +10.5 | +4.0 | −2.5 | −8.4 | −13.0 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: One disc in the 0.20 mol/dm³ solution had a starting mass of 2.40 g and a final mass of 2.34 g. Calculate its percentage change in mass.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe the effect of salt concentration on the change in mass of the discs.

points.description: As concentration increases, the change in mass decreases / discs gain less and then lose more mass
Gain in mass at 0.00 and 0.10 mol/dm³; loss at 0.20 mol/dm³ and above (quoting data, e.g. +10.5% to −13.0%)

parts.explanation: As the salt concentration increases, the change in mass falls steadily from +10.5% at 0.00 mol/dm³ to −13.0% at 0.40 mol/dm³. The discs gain mass in 0.00 and 0.10 mol/dm³ but lose mass at 0.20 mol/dm³ and above.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Use the results to estimate the salt concentration at which the discs would not change in mass.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the discs in the 0.40 mol/dm³ solution lost mass.

points.description: The solution was more concentrated than the cell sap / had a lower water potential than the cells
So water left the cells by osmosis through the partially permeable cell membranes

parts.explanation: The 0.40 mol/dm³ salt solution was more concentrated than the carrot cell sap (lower water potential), so water moved out of the cells by osmosis, through their partially permeable membranes, and the discs lost mass.

explanation: The change in mass falls as the salt concentration rises. Between 0.10 mol/dm³ (+4.0%) and 0.20 mol/dm³ (−2.5%) the change passes through zero, at about 0.16 mol/dm³: there the solution is as concentrated as the cell sap, so there is no net movement of water.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Change $= 2.34 - 2.40 = -0.06\ \text{g}$; $\dfrac{-0.06}{2.40} \times 100 = -2.5\%$.
2. (c) Zero change lies between 0.10 (+4.0%) and 0.20 (−2.5%). A straight line between these points crosses zero at $0.10 + 0.10 \times \dfrac{4.0}{6.5} = 0.16\ \text{mol/dm}^3$ (a reading from a graph between 0.14 and 0.18 is accepted).
hints: For (c), find where the change in mass goes from positive to negative.

stem: On hot afternoons, the leaves of a maize crop droop (wilt). By the next morning they are upright again. Explain these observations. [4]

points.description: In the hot afternoon the plant loses water (by transpiration) faster than the roots absorb it
Leaf cells lose water / become soft (flaccid); the pressure of water inside the cells falls
So the cells no longer support the leaves and the leaves droop
At night water loss falls; water enters the cells by osmosis, they become firm (turgid) again and support the leaves

answerSpec.modelAnswer: In the heat of the afternoon the maize plant loses water from its leaves faster than its roots can take it in. The leaf cells lose water, become soft (flaccid) and no longer press against their cell walls, so the leaves lose their support and droop. During the cooler night far less water is lost, so the roots catch up: water moves into the leaf cells by osmosis, the cells become firm (turgid) again, and the pressure of water inside them pushes on the cell walls and holds the leaves up.

explanation: Non-woody parts of plants are supported by the pressure of water inside their cells. When cells lose water they lose this support and the plant wilts; when they regain water by osmosis, the support returns.
hints: What holds up a leaf that has no wood?
When does the plant lose water fastest?

stem: A farmer puts a large amount of fertiliser right next to the roots of some young cabbage plants. The next day the plants have wilted. What is the best explanation?

options.content: The fertiliser blocked the stomata of the leaves, so the plants could no longer photosynthesise.
options.rationale: Fertiliser in the soil does not reach the stomata.

options.content: The roots absorbed so much fertiliser that the cells burst.
options.rationale: Plant cells do not burst; their walls prevent it.

options.content: The fertiliser killed the leaves by active transport.
options.rationale: Active transport is a cell process, not a cause of death.

options.content: The soil water became more concentrated than the cell sap, so water left the roots by osmosis.
options.rationale: The plants lost water instead of gaining it.

explanation: Dissolved fertiliser made the soil water more concentrated than the cell sap of the roots. Water then moved out of the root cells by osmosis instead of in, so the plants could not replace the water they lost and wilted.
hints: Compare the concentration of the soil water with that of the cell sap.

stem: Onion epidermis cells are mounted in a concentrated sucrose solution and viewed with a microscope. The cytoplasm and membrane of each cell have pulled away from the cell wall. What fills the space between the cell wall and the membrane?

options.content: Air
options.rationale: The cells are surrounded by liquid; air does not enter.

options.content: Cell sap that leaked from the vacuole
options.rationale: Cell sap stays inside the shrunken vacuole, within the membrane.

options.content: Nothing: it is a vacuum
options.rationale: A vacuum cannot form; the space fills with liquid.

options.content: The sucrose solution from outside
options.rationale: The cell wall is fully permeable, so the outside solution passes through it.

explanation: The cells are plasmolysed: water has left by osmosis and the membrane has pulled away from the wall. Because the cell wall is fully permeable, the outside sucrose solution passes through it and fills the space.
hints: Is the cell wall partially permeable or fully permeable?

stem: Salted, dried fish can be kept for months without going bad. Why does the salt help to preserve it?

options.content: Salt kills bacteria by reacting with them and making them too hot.
options.rationale: Salt does not raise the temperature.

options.content: Water leaves any bacteria or fungi on the fish by osmosis, so they cannot grow.
options.rationale: Salty surroundings are more concentrated than the microbes' cytoplasm.

options.content: Salt is a food that bacteria cannot digest.
options.rationale: Salt is not a food for bacteria.

options.content: Salt adds water to the fish by osmosis, which washes the bacteria away.
options.rationale: Salt draws water out; it does not add it.

explanation: A salty surface is much more concentrated than the cytoplasm of bacteria and fungi. Water leaves their cells by osmosis, so they cannot grow and cause decay.

stem: True or false: a solution with a high concentration of sucrose has a high water potential.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. Dissolving solute lowers water potential, so a concentrated solution has a low water potential.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. A concentrated solution has a low water potential; pure water has the highest.

explanation: Pure water has the highest water potential. The more solute is dissolved, the lower the water potential, so a concentrated sucrose solution has a low water potential.
hints: Which has the highest water potential of all?

stem:
Three bags of Visking tubing, A, B and C, were set up as shown and weighed after 30 minutes.

| Bag | Liquid inside the bag | Liquid in the beaker | Change in mass of bag / g |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 10% sucrose solution | Distilled water | +2.6 |
| B | Distilled water | 10% sucrose solution | −2.4 |
| C | 10% sucrose solution | 10% sucrose solution | 0.0 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which bag acted as a control?

options.content: A
options.rationale: Bag A has a concentration difference across the tubing.

options.content: C
options.rationale: Both sides have the same concentration, so it shows what happens with no concentration difference.

options.content: B
options.rationale: Bag B has a concentration difference across the tubing.

options.content: None of them
options.rationale: Bag C is a control.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why bag A gained mass.

points.description: The sucrose solution inside was more concentrated than the water outside
So water moved into the bag by osmosis through the partially permeable tubing

parts.explanation: The 10% sucrose solution inside bag A was more concentrated than the distilled water outside, so water moved into the bag by osmosis through the partially permeable Visking tubing.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why bag C did not change in mass, even though water molecules were still moving through the tubing.

points.description: Same concentration on both sides / no concentration gradient
Water molecules moved in and out at the same rate, so there was no net movement

parts.explanation: The solutions inside and outside bag C had the same concentration. Water molecules kept moving through the tubing in both directions, but at equal rates, so there was no net movement of water and no change in mass.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest why the mass of bag B decreased but no sucrose entered it.

points.description: Sucrose molecules are too large to pass through the partially permeable tubing (only water can cross)

parts.explanation: Water left bag B by osmosis into the more concentrated sucrose solution, but sucrose molecules are too large to pass through the tubing, so none entered.

explanation: Water moves by osmosis towards the more concentrated solution: into A and out of B. With equal concentrations (C) there is no net movement. Sucrose molecules cannot cross the tubing.
hints: In which bag is there no difference in concentration?

stem: Two neighbouring plant cells, X and Y, are separated by their cell membranes. The cell sap of X contains 0.3 mol/dm³ sucrose and the cell sap of Y contains 0.5 mol/dm³ sucrose. Which way will water move?

options.content: From X to Y, because X is more dilute
options.rationale: Water moves from the more dilute solution to the more concentrated one.

options.content: From Y to X, because Y is more concentrated
options.rationale: Water moves towards, not away from, the more concentrated solution.

options.content: Sucrose will move from Y to X instead of water
options.rationale: Sucrose cannot pass through the partially permeable membranes.

options.content: There will be no movement, because plant cells have walls
options.rationale: Cell walls are fully permeable and do not stop osmosis.

explanation: Cell X has the more dilute sap (0.3 mol/dm³), so water moves by osmosis from X into Y, which is more concentrated (0.5 mol/dm³).
hints: Water moves towards the more concentrated solution.

stem: Name the condition of a plant cell in which, after a lot of water loss, the cytoplasm and cell membrane have pulled away from the cell wall.

rejected.feedback: A flaccid cell is soft, but its membrane still touches the wall; pulling away from the wall is plasmolysis.
A turgid cell is full of water.
Wilting describes the whole plant drooping.

explanation: When a plant cell loses a lot of water by osmosis, the cytoplasm and membrane shrink away from the wall: the cell is plasmolysed.
hints: The name of this condition ends in -lysis.
